newsitem.title: GERMANY: SPD set against cut in top rate of German tax.
newsitem.headline: SPD set against cut in top rate of German tax.

text.p: Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD) said on Monday there was no room to cut the top rate of income tax under government plans for a radical overhaul of the country's tax system.

Speaking a week before Chancellor Helmut Kohl meets SPD chiefs for a tax summit, SPD manager Franz Muentefering said the arithmetic behind coalition plans to reduce the top tax bracket to 39 percent from 53 percent did not add up.
"It is not clear how that would be financed," Muentefering told reporters after a meeting of SPD leaders.

Despite massive differences, both sides are trying to find a compromise to remodel Germany's burdensome tax system. That would avoid lengthy arbitration in parliament, where the SPD can veto some tax measures with its the upper house majority.

Muentefering said it was wrong to focus on the issue of top rate income tax. Far more important, he said, was fighting high unemployment by cutting labour overheads and reducing the income tax burden on ordinary families and workers.
The SPD came under fire from the Free Democrats (FDP), the pro-business junior partner in Kohl's 14-year-old coalition, for not putting its own tax proposals on the table.
"It is not enough when the SPD always just says 'no'," FDP general secretary Guido Westerwelle told reporters.
Westerwelle said his party still supported a cut in the top income tax rate to below 40 percent, but added the coalition was going into the talks without setting any preconditions.

One aspect on which the FDP and SPD both agree is the need to bring forward the tax reforms to next year, so that Germany can step up the battle against unemployment which hit nearly 4.7 million in January, the highest since the 1930s depression.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel, leader of the Christian Social Union (CSU), Bavarian sister party to Kohl's Christian Democrats, last week said he was prepared to make some income tax cuts in 1998. But he stopped short of agreeing to implement all planned the cuts before elections due by autumn 1998.

With government-opposition horse-trading ahead, one leading government advisor on Monday warned against watering down Waigel's package, which would cut a net 30 billion marks in income and corporate taxes.

Rolf Peffekoven, one of the "five wise men" panel of independent economic advisors, said Kohl should make "no compromises" on cutting top-rate income tax if Germany is to attract new foreign investment.
"I say down with the top tax rate, and I also say the high rates must be lowered to the standard international level and that is clearly under 40 percent," he told Saarland radio.

Peffekoven said the cuts sought by the SPD would have little impact on Germany's sluggish economy. "We need investments and investments are predominantly financed by those with high incomes," he added.
Commentators welcomed the planned talks, but warned that they could easily fall prey to pre-election manoeuvring.
"Considering the alarming economic situation it is worth an attempt by the government and opposition to reach a quick and unconventional understanding," the Handelsblatt daily wrote.
"But there are too many tactics in play. In their efforts to position themselves favourably for 1998, an election year, the parties will probably lose sight of the problem."
